source: Shin, Polyanskaya, Lucero, Oulasvirta (2025) No Evidence for LLMs Being Useful in Problem Reframing (CHI 2025)
finding: Controlled test of whether LLM help improves problem frames written in Dorst's frame template. Three LLM modes were tried: direct frame generation, free-form chat, and a structured version of Dorst's nine-step process. None beat working without an LLM on frame novelty or usefulness.
numbers: 456 recruited, 280 kept after filters (218 in the pooled LLM group, so about 62 manual). Between-subjects, 4 arms. GPT-4o only. 3 design problems (aging, misbehavior, preference conflict). Each person submitted their 2 best frames; the 280 chosen frames were rated by expert peers (36 frames each) on novelty and usefulness. Mann-Whitney and Kruskal-Wallis, Dunn post hoc with Bonferroni; no significant quality difference. Power analysis: 220 and 280 participants needed for medium effects at 95% power.
quote: using LLMs does not help designers create better problem frames
limits: Null result from non-parametric tests with no equivalence test, so 'no evidence of benefit' is not proof of no benefit. One model (GPT-4o), fixed button-driven prompts, crowd workers paid 16 euros for an hour, told to submit their best frames. Authors say LLM frames were often too weak to build on.
agent_relevance: Strong prior that a bolt-on reframe step does not help by itself. Keep O8 gated and test it as an arm against equal-token plain resampling.

source: Shin, Polyanskaya, Lucero, Oulasvirta (2025) No Evidence for LLMs Being Useful in Problem Reframing (CHI 2025) - perceived help and expertise
finding: Perceived help and real help came apart. People rated the LLMs as moderately to well supportive, yet frame quality did not rise. Within the LLM arms, people who understood reframing better made more novel frames and felt more agency.
numbers: CSI (creativity support index) for all three LLM arms fell in the moderate-to-good range. Experts vs novices, LLM frames: novelty 12.54% higher for experts (p=0.01); in the free-form arm 20.84% higher, p=0.06 (not significant). Agency: experts higher (p=0.04); in the structured arm 15.69% higher (p=0.02). Usefulness and ownership gaps all p>0.05. Expertise measured by a 5-question quiz on reframing concepts; balance across arms chi2(3, N=280)=0.70, p=0.87.
limits: Expert/novice split is by quiz, not by years of practice. The gap is seen for novelty only, not usefulness. The passages read give no manual-arm comparison of the gap, so we cannot say LLMs widen the gap versus no LLM.
agent_relevance: A feeling of progress from a reframe step is not evidence of progress. Judge reframes by outputs, in line with guardrail G10.

source: Shin, Polyanskaya, Lucero, Oulasvirta (2025) No Evidence for LLMs Being Useful in Problem Reframing (CHI 2025) - what participants did with the LLM
finding: Participants who used LLMs mostly complained that the LLM frames were not novel, were repetitive or were not useful. They regenerated output often. The structured Dorst process took longest.
numbers: 93 of 218 LLM users reported trouble building on LLM ideas: not novel n=31, repetitive n=14, not useful n=12. Mean time to make 2 frames: manual 23.25 min, direct 21.82, structured 28.35, free-form 20.78. In the structured arm all but one participant regenerated all content at least once; the apparent-problem step was regenerated by 39 people and the stakeholder step by 25.
limits: Self-reported reasons from a subset of users; no coding reliability given in the text read.
agent_relevance: Frames from a language model tend to be one typical answer. Same problem as typical-answer fixation. Pair a reframe step with forced distance from the first frame.

source: Shin, Polyanskaya, Lucero, Oulasvirta (2025) No Evidence for LLMs Being Useful in Problem Reframing (CHI 2025) - the Dorst template and process as implemented
finding: The paper gives an operational form of Dorst's reframing. Frame template: 'If the problem of X is approached as if Y, then the direction of solutions could be Z'. Process: destructure (apparent problems, ineffective solutions, paradoxical problems), explore stakeholders and their views, synthesise themes, generate frames, assess frames for usefulness and feasibility.
numbers: Nine steps in the study: three destructuring steps, three stakeholder steps, then themes, frames, assessment. Slow-elevator example: complaint 'elevators too slow'; the frame shifts from speed to the waiting experience; the fix is a better waiting area.
quote: If the problem of {initial problem} is approached as if {alternative perspective}, then the direction of solutions could be {potential solutions}
limits: This is the authors' reading of Dorst 2015, not Dorst's own text. Dorst's own step names were not opened. The interface reversed the order of the last two steps (LLM assesses before frames are written).
agent_relevance: A frame can be a typed record (problem, as-if view, solution direction) that code can diff against the old frame. That fits the plan in SUBFIELDS.md.

source: Zheng, Mishra, Chen, Cheng, Chi, Le, Zhou (2023/2024) Take a Step Back: Evoking Reasoning via Abstraction in LLMs (ICLR 2024)
finding: Step-back prompting: first ask a more abstract question (which principles apply?), then reason from the answer. This is a re-representation step done by the model itself. It beat chain of thought on physics and chemistry.
numbers: MMLU Physics: PaLM-2L 66.4 -> 73.2; GPT-4 69.4 -> 84.5; Llama2-70B 51.9 -> 64.8 (5 runs, SD 1 to 2 points). MMLU Chemistry: PaLM-2L 70.9 -> 81.8; GPT-4 80.9 -> 85.6; Llama2-70B 55.7 -> 66.7. Zero-shot chain of thought on PaLM-2L physics 65.0 and take-a-deep-breath 65.7 (no gain over 66.4).
limits: Abstraction is not Dorst reframing; it retrieves general principles but does not question the goal. Few-shot demos of step-back questions were written per task. Gains are method and model specific.
agent_relevance: Cheap, tested relative of O8: an abstraction question before solving. Good first A/B arm because it needs no judge.

source: Zheng, Mishra, Chen, Cheng, Chi, Le, Zhou (2023/2024) Take a Step Back: Evoking Reasoning via Abstraction in LLMs (ICLR 2024) - knowledge QA and multi-hop
finding: Step-back (with and without retrieval) gave big gains where details mislead lookup, and no gain where the baseline was already high.
numbers: PaLM-2L. TimeQA: base 41.5; zero-shot CoT 40.8; RAG 57.4; step-back alone 66.0; step-back + RAG 68.7 (GPT-4 base 45.6). TimeQA Easy: 42.6; RAG 67.8; step-back 70.4; both 75.2. MuSiQue: base 35.5; CoT 38.7; RAG 39.6; step-back 42.6; both 42.8. StrategyQA: base 82.8; CoT 83.6; RAG 84.2; step-back alone 82.7 (no change); both 86.4.
limits: Column assignment read from table row order in the PDF text; check against the paper before quoting. High-baseline StrategyQA shows no gain from step-back alone.
agent_relevance: Spend the abstraction step where the task has many details and a lookup step. Skip it where the baseline already works (G12).

source: Zheng, Mishra, Chen, Cheng, Chi, Le, Zhou (2023/2024) Take a Step Back: Evoking Reasoning via Abstraction in LLMs (ICLR 2024) - error analysis
finding: Step-back fixes some baseline errors but also adds new ones. After abstraction, most remaining errors are reasoning errors, not abstraction errors.
numbers: MMLU high-school physics: corrects 20.5% of baseline errors and introduces 11.9% new errors. More than 90% of remaining errors are in the reasoning step; principle (abstraction) errors are a small share. TimeQA: step-back+RAG fixes 39.9% of baseline errors and causes 5.6% new ones. StrategyQA: fixes 15.4% and causes 6.1% new ones.
limits: Error classes were hand-annotated by the authors on the test set.
agent_relevance: A reframe step has a cost: it breaks some answers that were right. Gate it by a check, not by default.

source: Deng, Zhang, Chen, Gu (2023/2024) Rephrase and Respond: Let LLMs Ask Better Questions for Themselves
finding: Let the model rewrite the human's question in its own words, then answer. The authors link this to 'frames in thought': the model and the asker hold different frames and the mismatch causes errors.
numbers: GPT-4 zero-shot accuracy, original -> one-step RaR: Day 54.29 -> 93.33; Month 58.10 -> 83.96; Year 57.14 -> 89.52; Last-letter (2 words) 52.05 -> 99.09; Last-letter (4) 21.36 -> 86.82; Coin flip 74.55 -> 99.09; CSQA 84.09 -> 85.45; Age 98.44 -> 100 (ceiling). Subsets of 220 per task (Dates uses all).
limits: Largest gains are on questions that are ambiguous as written, so part of the gain is repair of poor wording. Gains are larger for GPT-4 than for GPT-3.5 and Vicuna-13b. Not a test of goal change.
agent_relevance: Rewrite the task statement in the model's own terms before attempting it: cheap, helps mainly when the stated task is unclear. Treat as S1 input hygiene, not as O8.

source: Mishra, Khashabi, Baral, Choi, Hajishirzi (2022) Reframing Instructional Prompts to GPT-k's Language (ACL Findings)
finding: Hand-written reframing of instructions into short, concrete, step-split prompts helped older GPT models across 12 NLP tasks. Methods: decompose a task into sub-tasks, itemise steps, use concrete wording, cut abstract background statements.
numbers: 12 tasks in 6 categories. Few-shot gain from the same reframed prompts: GPT-3 series +12.5% on average, GPT-2 series +6.7%. Reframing also cut the number of examples needed in few-shot prompting.
limits: Older models (GPT-2, GPT-3 series). Reframing was manual and the authors say instruction reframing is not algorithmic. This is rewording, not Dorst-style frame change; gains may fade on strong instruction-tuned models.
agent_relevance: Same idea as G11 and task decomposition: split the task. Do not expect large gains on current frontier models without a fresh test.

source: Sharma et al. (2023) Cognitive Reframing of Negative Thoughts through Human-Language Model Interaction (ACL 2023)
finding: A clinical meaning of reframing: replace a negative thought by a more hopeful one. The paper defines 7 linguistic attributes of a reframe, trains a retrieval-enhanced model on 600 practitioner examples, and tests which attributes people prefer in a field study.
numbers: Field study: 2,067 website visitors, one month. Highly empathic reframes preferred 39.7% vs 25.5% of the time (55.7% more often, p<1e-5). Highly positive reframes preferred less (29.6% vs 38.3%). More rational reframes rated 10.8% more relatable (3.91 vs 3.53, p<0.05). Reframes that address a thinking trap were 6.3% more helpful (3.39 vs 3.19, p<0.01). Safety filter flagged 32 of 5,760 suggestions (0.56%).
limits: Different construct from design framing; outcome is a self-rating, not a solved problem. Percent gains are on Likert means.
agent_relevance: Weak link only. Shows that reframe attributes (specific, actionable, not over-positive) predict acceptance. Not evidence that reframing improves task accuracy.

source: Jiang, Ilievski, Ma, Sourati (2023) BRAINTEASER: Lateral Thinking Puzzles for LLMs (EMNLP 2023)
finding: Lateral thinking puzzles need the solver to drop the default reading (a reframe). Models are far below people, and they drop sharply when the same puzzle is reworded or moved to a new context, which points to memorised answers rather than a new frame.
numbers: 1,100 puzzles (sentence and word types). ChatGPT 53% and 63% on the two subtasks vs random 25% and human 92%. Annotators rated 99% of 102 sampled originals valid (Fleiss kappa 0.948). ChatGPT and RoBERTa-L fail 45% and 61% of originals or semantic variants that they solve in the context-rewritten version. About a third of models are at or below random.
limits: Multiple-choice format makes it easier than open puzzles; in the open-ended try people (2.64/5) and ChatGPT (2.62/5) both did poorly. 2023 models; current reasoning models are not covered here.
agent_relevance: The repo's BRAINTEASER item is the closest ready test of a reframe step. Measure group-consistency over reworded variants, not only single-item accuracy.

source: Weak-eval-Strong: Evaluating and Eliciting Lateral Thinking of LLMs with Situation Puzzles (NeurIPS 2024, SPLAT)
finding: A situation-puzzle benchmark with a multi-turn yes/no judge. Reasoning prompts built from the benchmark also lifted performance a little on other lateral-thinking sets.
numbers: A weaker judge model (WizardLM-2) agrees with humans over 80% on intermediate and final answers. RiddleSense: Llama3-70B 83.34 -> 85.21, Llama3-8B 70.51 -> 72.18, GPT-4 88.83 -> 89.23. Three difficulty levels (easy, medium, hard).
limits: Gains on transfer sets are small (about 0.4 to 1.9 points). The authors say puzzles that need no judge help are closer to knowledge tests than lateral thinking.
agent_relevance: Small consistent gains from a guided question loop. Guided probing may beat silent re-reading, but the gain is small.

source: Sotnikova et al. (2026) CresOWLve: Benchmarking Creative Problem-Solving Over Real-World Knowledge (COLM 2026)
finding: 2,061 puzzles from a Russian quiz game need facts plus creative links. Models do worse on creative questions than on factual sub-questions of the same puzzle.
numbers: Up to 17% drop between factual and creative questions across frontier thinking and non-thinking models (abstract). Five difficulty levels. No formal human evaluation was run.
limits: Only the abstract, setup and limits were read; the model-by-model table was not extracted. Not a framing test as such.
agent_relevance: Creative linking, not fact recall, is where models lose. Score a reframe step on the link, not only final accuracy.

source: Wadinambiarachchi, Kelly, Pareek, Zhou, Velloso (2024) The Effects of Generative AI on Design Fixation and Divergent Thinking (CHI 2024)
finding: Fixation is the human-side opposite of reframing. People shown an example and given AI images copied more of the example, and made fewer ideas with less variety and originality, than people with no support.
numbers: N=60 between participants; 14 salient features in the example avatar. Design fixation score: GenAI +0.32 (89% CI 0.11 to 0.55, Bayes factor 124); image search +0.27 (CI 0.05 to 0.49, Bayes factor 42.5) versus no support.
limits: Bayesian multilevel model, small sample, one task (chatbot avatar sketching), Midjourney only.
agent_relevance: Seeing one typical output narrows later output. Supports fresh-context attempts and forced distance between attempts.

source: Carichon et al. (2026) IDEAFix: Evaluation Framework for Creative Defixation Prompting in LLMs
finding: 81 design briefs and 25 prompts drawn from 6 creativity methods (brainstorming, C-K theory, TRIZ, design thinking, scenarios, SCAMPER) plus 4 AI-specific 'category negation' prompts. Short 'think outside the box' style prompts did as well as or better than method-heavy prompts. All 5 models stayed homogenised.
numbers: Models: Llama-3.1-70B, Qwen3-30B, Gemini-2.5-Flash, GPT-4o, Grok-4.1-fast. Briefs: 26 products, 15 services, 26 strategies, 14 procedures. Best strategies lifted novelty and rarity by roughly 10 to 41% over control depending on metric (read from chart labels, not from a table).
limits: Automatic embedding-distance metrics, no human raters. Percent figures were read from a chart and may be matched to the wrong bars. Task is idea generation, not reframing.
agent_relevance: Complex human methods did not beat plain divergence instructions. Do not copy design-method procedures into prompts without a test.

source: Wang et al. (2026) NexusAI: Design Space Exploration through Cognitive Abstraction and Functional Decomposition
finding: A tool turns LLM ideas into typed pieces (what, how, value) at several abstraction levels so users can recombine them. In a small study users reported more control and more movement beyond first ideas than with a baseline canvas.
numbers: 14 participants. Coverage 0.407 vs 0.079 (p=0.004); coherence-to-prompt 0.274 vs 0.053 (p=0.009). Self-ratings: move beyond initial thinking 6.14 vs 4.19 (p=0.006); steer directions 6.29 vs 3.94 (p=0.002).
limits: Only 14 people, mostly self-ratings, against a node-canvas baseline with basic AI generation; no solution-quality rating in the parts read.
agent_relevance: A typed breakdown of an idea into what, how and value is a concrete data shape for a frame record.

source: Tracing Cognitive Processes in Insight Problem Solving: Using GAMs and Change Point Analysis (J. Intelligence 2023)
finding: Insight (human restructuring) in matchstick arithmetic: the representation change looks sudden in eye movements, but ordinary ANOVA hides it. Non-linear models find a jump near the end of the solving period.
numbers: 61 participants. Only 34% solved the matchstick problem alone; 11% more solved it after a hint. Solving time split into 10 bins; the change point for solvers falls near the 90% bin. ANOVA predicted the shift earlier (80% bin) than the raw data.
limits: One problem type, eye tracking, small N. Representational change theory is described secondhand here, not tested head-on.
agent_relevance: Real frame changes in humans look abrupt, not gradual. A loop that adds small edits each round may never produce one.

source: Korovkin, Vladimirov, Chistopolskaya, Savinova (2018) How Working Memory Provides Representational Change During Insight Problem Solving (Front. Psychol.)
finding: Dual-task probes show insight problems load working memory storage, while non-insight problems load the control system. The paper restates RCT: insight is a change of problem representation.
numbers: Dual-task paradigm with verbal and visual probe tasks at several solving stages; two experiments. Cites (does not report) a finding that higher working memory capacity goes with lower matchstick accuracy because it inhibits constraint relaxation.
limits: The capacity-accuracy link is cited, not measured here. The authors call the load dynamics in insight problems 'debatable'.
agent_relevance: More held context does not help a reframe and can hold the old frame in place (see the Einstellung subfield).

source: Chunk decomposition and reorganisation with Chinese characters (Front. Psychol. 2017), D-process versus R-process
finding: Breaking a familiar chunk is easy; reassembling the parts into a new chunk is the hard step. This challenges the claim, from Knoblich's matchstick work, that decomposition itself is the main difficulty.
numbers: 60 students, two task sets. Decomposition accuracy about 98.4% (radical removal) vs reorganisation about 62.2%; task effect F(1,24)=205.23, p<0.001 on accuracy and F(1,24)=45.77, p<0.001 on reaction time. Radical removal 1,797 ms vs stroke removal 3,070 ms.
limits: Chinese characters are not matchsticks. The authors say the control condition in Knoblich's original work may explain why chunk level mattered there but not here.
agent_relevance: Two-part model of a reframe: break the old frame, then rebuild a new one. A prompt that only asks for 'a different view' tests the first part, not the second.

source: Schon (1983) The Reflective Practitioner
finding: Not opened this session; stated from memory of the literature. Practice is a reflective conversation with the situation. The practitioner 'sets' the problem by naming what to attend to and framing the context. The situation talks back; surprise triggers reflection-in-action and a reframe. A frame is tested by moves, and the practitioner asks whether the consequences are acceptable.
numbers: None; case studies (architecture studio, psychotherapy, town planning). Shin et al. 2025 (opened) restates Schon as 'a reflective practice of sense-making' where designers redefine the nature of problems and solutions.
limits: Case-based essay, no controlled test. Used here only as a description of practice.
agent_relevance: Let real check output (back-talk) trigger O8, not a timer. Mirrors the schema's rule that a failing output names the framing first.

source: Schon (1979) Generative metaphor: a perspective on problem-setting in social policy
finding: Not opened this session; stated from memory of the literature. Policy stories carry hidden metaphors that set the problem. Classic case: urban blight seen as a disease to cut out vs seen as a natural community to keep. The same facts support opposite fixes.
numbers: None; qualitative case.
limits: Single illustrative case, not tested experimentally.
agent_relevance: A reframe often shows up as a change in the main metaphor. Ask the agent to name the metaphor of the current frame.

source: Schon and Rein (1994) Frame Reflection: Toward the Resolution of Intractable Policy Controversies
finding: Not opened this session; stated from memory of the literature. Policy disputes persist because each side holds a different frame. Facts alone do not settle them. Progress needs reflection on the frames, not argument inside one.
numbers: None; policy case studies.
limits: Qualitative; the claim that frame reflection resolves disputes was not tested here.
agent_relevance: When two good attempts disagree, compare their frames, not their answers.

source: Dorst (2011) The core of design thinking and its application (Design Studies 32(6))
finding: Not opened this session; stated from memory of the literature. The core logic of design is abduction. Given a desired value, the designer must find both a 'what' (object or service) and a 'how' (working principle), unlike deduction, where both are known. Frames bridge that gap: 'if we look at the problem as if it is X, then working principle Y gives value Z'.
numbers: No numbers. Semantic Scholar showed about 1,757 citations in a search call this session (count only).
limits: Theory paper; the claim that this is the 'core' of design thinking has no direct experiment behind it.
agent_relevance: A frame is a pair: a viewpoint and a working principle. Store both, not just a reworded task.

source: Dorst (2015) Frame Innovation: Create New Thinking by Design (MIT Press)
finding: Not opened this session; stated from memory of the literature. Nine-step frame creation model for open, complex, networked problems: dig into the problem history, find the paradox, study the stakeholder context and themes, then build and test frames and their futures. Built from practitioner case work.
numbers: None checked. Shin et al. 2025 (opened) implements it as: apparent problems, ineffective solutions, paradoxical problems, stakeholders (current, potential, their views), themes, frames, assessment.
limits: Practice-derived model. No controlled study of its benefit has been opened; the first controlled test read (Shin 2025, N=280) is null for LLM help. DOI confirmed by a Crossref lookup only.
agent_relevance: The paradox step (why is the obvious fix blocked?) is the one concrete, checkable move; it can be an S-state trigger.

source: Paton and Dorst (2011) Briefing and reframing: A situated practice (Design Studies 32(6))
finding: Not opened this session; stated from memory of the literature. Study of professional designers at the briefing stage: reframing happens in conversation with the client and context, through themes, not as a lone act of invention.
numbers: Numbers not checked.
limits: Qualitative field study, small sample, not opened.
agent_relevance: Reframing is set off by new information from outside; an agent with no new checks has little to reframe against.

source: Valkenburg and Dorst (1998) The reflective practice of design teams (Design Studies 19(3))
finding: Not opened this session; stated from memory of the literature. Applied Schon's moves (naming, framing, moving, reflecting) to coded recordings of student design teams.
numbers: Numbers not checked.
limits: Few teams, coded by the authors, not opened. Findings about which teams did better are not confirmed here.
agent_relevance: Count how often the agent frames versus moves; a log of frame changes is a cheap diagnostic.

source: Lawson (1979) study of architects and scientists on a block-arrangement task (problem-focused vs solution-focused)
finding: Not opened this session; stated from memory of the literature. Scientists tended to work by learning the hidden rule (problem-focused); architects tended to try solutions and learn the problem from failed ones (solution-focused). Basis for the claim that designers learn the problem by proposing solutions.
numbers: Numbers not checked.
limits: Small samples from two professions, one lab task, confounded with training; not opened. Later co-evolution work (subfield 03) builds on it.
agent_relevance: See subfield 03 on co-evolution; a failed solution is information about the frame.

source: Kaplan and Simon (1990) In search of insight (Cognitive Psychology 22), mutilated checkerboard
finding: Not opened this session; stated from memory of the literature. Insight on the mutilated checkerboard needs the solver to search the space of problem representations, not only the space of moves. Making the parity cue visible shortens solving.
numbers: Numbers not checked.
limits: Single task; many solvers never find the invariant; not opened.
agent_relevance: Two search spaces: moves and representations. O8 is search in the second.

source: Knoblich, Ohlsson, Haider, Rhenius (1999) Constraint relaxation and chunk decomposition in insight problem solving (JEP: LMC 25)
finding: Not opened this session; stated from memory of the literature. Matchstick arithmetic: tight constraints on what may change and the need to break familiar chunks make a problem hard. The Chinese-character paper (opened) restates one result: turning XI = III + III into VI = III + III is harder than turning IV = III + III into VI = III + II.
numbers: Sample sizes and solution rates not checked.
limits: Extended in other labs; one extension (opened) did not find the chunk-level effect in new material.
agent_relevance: Constraint relaxation is a named operation: list the assumed constraints and drop one.

source: Rittel and Webber (1973) Dilemmas in a general theory of planning (Policy Sciences 4)
finding: Not opened this session; stated from memory of the literature. Wicked problems have no definitive formulation; the way the problem is stated already shapes the solution. Every formulation of the problem corresponds to a particular solution.
numbers: None; ten properties of wicked problems.
limits: Essay.
agent_relevance: Fits the role of O8: if the statement of the problem fixes the solution class, change the statement.

source: Roozenburg (2002) on design reasoning as abduction; Kolko (2010) Abductive thinking and sensemaking
finding: Not opened this session; stated from memory of the literature. Design reasoning is abductive: from a desired result, infer a plausible what and how. Kolko describes designers building frames by abductive sensemaking from messy data.
numbers: None.
limits: Conceptual; named only because Dorst 2011 builds on abduction forms from Roozenburg. Exact citation details not checked.
agent_relevance: Reframes are guesses to be tested, not deductions; plan a test for each.
